items.text: The API is stateless; your code keeps the history list
Append the question **and** the reply, every turn
Input tokens, and cost, grow with every turn
Trim in user and assistant pairs, or summarise

captions.text: Every chat app and every agent is a conversation: a list of messages that grows over
time.
In this lesson you'll see that the API remembers nothing, that your code owns the
history, and that a growing history means a growing bill.
You'll build a multi-turn conversation correctly.
Spot and fix the classic forgotten reply bug.
Measure how input tokens grow with every turn.
And choose a strategy for keeping long conversations under control.
Here's how a conversation really works.
The first request contains one user message.
The API replies, and then forgets everything.
Your app stores the user message and the reply in a list.
The second request sends the whole list: the first question, the first reply, and
the new question.
And the third request sends five messages.
Roles alternate between user and assistant, and the first message is always from the
user.
The history is just a Python list of message dictionaries.
For each question, we append it to the history, and send the whole list as messages.
Then we append the assistant's reply.
This line is the one people forget.
Finally we print how many messages we sent, and how many input tokens that cost.
Look at the numbers.
One message, then three, then five.
And the input tokens grow every turn, because every request re-sends everything
before it.
The offline fake even reports how many earlier messages it received, so you can see
the history arriving.
Here's the classic bug.
The loop appends each question, but never the reply.
So the history contains two user messages in a row.
The API accepts that, and merges them into a single user turn.
But the model never sees what it said before, so it can't refer to its own earlier
answers.
User, user.
No assistant turn.
In a chat app, that shows up as an assistant that seems to have amnesia.
Always store the reply right after you receive it.
Since every turn re-sends the whole history, long conversations get slower and more
expensive, and eventually hit the context window.
There are a few standard strategies.
The simplest is a sliding window: keep the most recent turns, and drop the oldest
user and assistant pair once you're over a budget.
Our project does this.
A smarter option replaces old turns with a short summary written by the model.
That's part of Module 6 on memory.
And agents often store key facts in a database, and add back only what's relevant to
the current question.
Finally, prompt caching lets an unchanged prefix of the conversation be billed at a
large discount when you re-send it.
You'll use it later in the course.
One practical rule when trimming.
Drop messages in pairs, a user message and its reply together, so the roles keep
alternating and the history still starts with a user turn.
Quick check.
A conversation already has ten messages.
How many messages does your next request send?
Eleven: all ten earlier messages plus the new one, unless you deliberately trim the
history.
The API is stateless, and your code keeps the history.
Append both the question and the reply, every turn.
Input tokens, and cost, grow with every turn.
So trim in pairs, or summarise, to keep conversations under control.
Next, you'll control the output itself: length limits, streaming, and structured
JSON.
